heading: Step 4: Call the server from the page
body:
This step is shown in JavaScript and TypeScript. In the other Tac languages, an HTTPClient cannot yet send a request from the browser to the server, so skip to step 5 if you chose one of them. A client class sends HTTP requests for the page. Put it in `client/clients`. `HTTPClient` marks the class. `GetRequest("/api/greeting")` makes the method `getGreeting` send a GET request to the controller of step 3. Leave the method body empty: Tachyon writes it. An empty body returns nothing to the type checker, so the method declares its answer as `Promise<Greeting | void>`. `export default` lets the type checker and the other classes find the client without an import.

In the service, `Needs` asks Tachyon to put a `GreetingClient` into the field `greetingClient`. The method `askServer` waits for the answer. The private method `messageOf` gives its message, or an empty text when there is no answer, and `askServer` saves it in the field `message`. A public method of a service holds no decision (TY1314), so the check sits in the private method. The page has its own copy of the model in `client/models/Greeting.ts`, because the browser cannot read files in `server/`. JavaScript reads its type with `/** @import { Greeting } from '/models/Greeting.ts' */`. Change the component, the service and add the client. The page file stays the same as in step 2.

Result: click Ask the server. The text Hello from Yon appears under the buttons. A path such as `/api/greeting` stays on the same origin, so no host needs to be listed. A request to another host needs that host in `tac.outgoing.hosts`.
